erosion-and-rivers.title: Erosion and rivers
erosion-and-rivers.text: Erosion and rivers A relief read from a file stays as it is. The erosion rule lets it change: the land rises, the rivers cut their valleys deeper and the hillslopes round off, step after step, and the rivers come out of where the water gathers. The other plugins read the changed ground, its drainage and its rivers from the world. A made-up island at the start and after a million years: deeper valleys, sharper ridges, and the rivers drawn where the water gathers The example island ( examples/eroding-island.yaml ): each step stands for 10 000 years. The valleys deepen and branch, and the rivers grow longer as more ground drains into them. Put it after the relief rule: it starts from the elevation the world already has. - rule: relief with: {path: island.npy, minimum_x: -4, minimum_z: -4, cell_size: 0.05} - rule: erosion with: {years_per_unit: 10000, uplift: 0.0002, erodibility: 0.000002, random_receivers: true} The model The rule is a landscape evolution model of the usual kind (Tucker and Hancock 2010). Every cell of the ground follows dz/dt = U − K·A^m·S + κ·∇²z U, uplift ( uplift , metres a year): the land rises, all of it at the same pace. K·A^m·S, the stream power law (Howard 1994; Whipple and Tucker 1999): water cuts into the ground faster where more of it runs (A, the area that drains through the cell, stands for the discharge) and where it runs steeper (S, the slope towards the cell it goes to). K ( erodibility ) says how easily the rock gives way and m ( area_exponent ) how much the amount of water counts; the slope's exponent is 1. κ·∇²z, soil creep ( diffusivity , m² a year): hillslopes round off, because soil slowly moves from the convex tops to the concave feet (Fernandes and Dietrich 1997; Roering et al. 1999). The sea (ground at or below sea_level ) and the cells on the edge of the grid are the base level : they do not change, and every drop of water ends in one of them. A relief cut out of a larger map lets its rivers leave through the edges. How it is solved Every piece of time: Drainage. The hollows are filled for the water (priority flood, Barnes et al. 2014), so water from every cell reaches the base level, and each cell gives its water to its steepest lower neighbour of eight. The area drained adds up from the highest cells down. Uplift , on everything but the base level. Valleys. The stream power law is solved implicitly, from the lowest cells up (Braun and Willett 2013): it is stable for any length of time and a cell never ends lower than the cell its water goes to. A cell lower than that one lies in a hollow and is left alone, so the hollows of the relief stay where they are. Creep , with the four neighbours of each cell. Creep is only stable for short pieces of time (κ·Δt/Δx² ≤ 0.2), so a long step is cut into as many pieces as it needs. The heights are kept in float64 between steps: a change of a fraction of a millimetre a year would be lost if it were rounded to the float32 of the fields every year. Drawn receivers. Always sending the water to the steepest of eight neighbours cuts straight valleys lined up with the grid, which a shaded relief shows as stripes. With random_receivers , each cell sends its water to one of its lower neighbours drawn with a chance that grows with the square of its slope, so the valleys wander like real ones. The draws come from seed : the same seed, the same valleys. What a year means The numbers of the model are in metres and years, and years_per_unit says how many years of erosion each unit of the stage's clock stands for. With the default of 1, a year of the clock is a year of erosion, and the ground hardly moves: rivers lower their beds by tenths of a millimetre a year, so a town that grows for a century sees its ground change by centimetres at the most. To see valleys form, make every step stand for thousands of years ( years_per_unit: 10000 ), in a stage of its own before the stages that use the ground. What it publishes At the start and then every publish_every steps: What Kind Unit elevation , slope fields metres; rise over run drainage_area field km² of ground that drains through each cell (0 on the base level) rivers entities of kind river : a line with a width world units; properties width (world units) and drainage_area (km² where the river ends) A river starts where the drained area reaches river_area (channel heads drain from hundredths of a km² to about one; Montgomery and Dietrich 1988) and runs down to the sea, the edge or a bigger river. The rivers that drain most are traced first, so a main river keeps its whole length and its tributaries end where they meet it. Its width grows with the area it drains, as hydraulic geometry finds for the discharge (Leopold and Maddock 1953): width = river_width[0] · area^river_width[1] , 3 m · area(km²)^0.5 by default. The line goes through the cell centres, with its corners rounded (Chaikin 1974). Each river is named after the cell where it starts, so a river that only changes a little is modified, not replaced. Numbers The defaults are middle values from the literature; set them for your own place. Parameter Default Range in the literature erodibility 1e-5 a year⁻¹ (m = 0.5) about 1e-7 to 1e-4, from hard to soft rock (Stock and Montgomery 1999; Harel et al. 2016) area_exponent 0.5 concavity m/n of 0.3 to 0.7, 0.5 most often (Whipple and Tucker 1999) diffusivity 0.005 m² a year 0.001 to 0.01 m² a year on soil-mantled hillslopes (Fernandes and Dietrich 1997; Roering et al. 1999) uplift 0 tenths of a millimetre to a few millimetres a year in active mountains river_area 1 km² channel heads drain from hundredths of a km² to about one (Montgomery and Dietrich 1988) river_width [3, 0.5] the exponent 0.5 is hydraulic geometry's (Leopold and Maddock 1953); the coefficient is a round value References Barnes, R., Lehman, C. and Mulla, D. (2014). Priority-flood: an optimal depression-filling and watershed-labeling algorithm for digital elevation models. Computers & Geosciences 62. Braun, J. and Willett, S. D. (2013). A very efficient O(n), implicit and parallel method to solve the stream power equation governing fluvial incision and landscape evolution. Geomorphology 180–181. Chaikin, G. M. (1974). An algorithm for high-speed curve generation. Computer Graphics and Image Processing 3. Fernandes, N. F. and Dietrich, W. E. (1997). Hillslope evolution by diffusive processes: the timescale for equilibrium adjustments. Water Resources Research 33. Harel, M.-A., Mudd, S. M. and Attal, M. (2016). Global analysis of the stream power law parameters based on worldwide ¹⁰Be denudation rates. Geomorphology 268. Howard, A. D. (1994). A detachment-limited model of drainage basin evolution. Water Resources Research 30. Leopold, L. B. and Maddock, T. (1953). The hydraulic geometry of stream channels and some physiographic implications. USGS Professional Paper 252. Montgomery, D. R. and Dietrich, W. E. (1988). Where do channels begin? Nature 336. Roering, J. J., Kirchner, J. W. and Dietrich, W. E. (1999). Evidence for nonlinear, diffusive sediment transport on hillslopes and implications for landscape morphology. Water Resources Research 35. Stock, J. D. and Montgomery, D. R. (1999). Geologic constraints on bedrock river incision using the stream power law. Journal of Geophysical Research 104. Tucker, G. E. and Hancock, G. R. (2010). Modelling landscape evolution. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms 35. Whipple, K. X. and Tucker, G. E. (1999). Dynamics of the stream-power river incision model. Journal of Geophysical Research 104.

getting-started.title: 🚀 Getting started
getting-started.text: 🚀 Getting started The folders it needs The plugin is developed next to Go Simulator and the libraries it uses: go.mod replaces them with the folders beside this one. Clone them side by side: go-simulator/ the host: runs the rules files go-simulator-terrain/ this plugin go-scene-builder/ reads relieve.json reliefs go-renderer/ used by go-simulator's viewer Running the example examples/ground.yaml starts the plugin and runs one stage whose only rule is relief : plugins: - name: terrain command: [go, run, .] directory: .. stages: - name: ground clock: {from: 0, to: 1, step: 1} snapshots: [1] rules: - rule: relief with: {path: relieve.json, origin: [0, 0]} Run it from Go Simulator without a window: cd ../go-simulator go run ./cmd/simulate -rules ../go-simulator-terrain/examples/ground.yaml -output results/ Relative paths start at the rules file's folder, so relieve.json is looked for in examples/ . Your own relief The example does not come with a relief. Put one next to it, either way: Go Scene Builder's relief : relieve.json and relieve.f32 side by side, placed on the world with origin . A NumPy array : a .npy of heights in metres, placed with minimum_x , minimum_z and cell_size . - rule: relief with: {path: relieve.json, origin: [6, 4.5]} - rule: relief with: {path: relief.npy, minimum_x: -1, minimum_z: -1, cell_size: 0.0125} (One rule or the other, not both.) Reliefs and fields explains every key, and the rules reference lists them all. What a run writes At every time a stage lists in snapshots , simulate writes each field as a grid: a JSON header and its values as little-endian float32, row by row, the relief format of Go Scene Builder. For the example, in results/ : File Content ground 1 elevation.json + .f32 the heights in metres, the relief's own values ground 1 slope.json + .f32 the slope of every cell, rise over run ground 1.geojson the entities with a ground shape (none from this plugin) events.jsonl the events (none from this plugin) The header gives columns , rows , cell and the extent in world units, so the files can be read back as a relief or drawn as a map, as the pictures in these pages were. The tests go vet ./... go test ./... The tests check both formats on small synthetic reliefs, the slope of a plane, and that the fields reach the world before the first step. For erosion they check that no water is lost or made on the way to the sea, that hollows drain, that uplift and erosion settle where the stream power law says (S = (U/K)·A^−m), that creep never overshoots however long the step, that the sea does not move, that the same seed gives the same valleys, that every rule describes its contracts, and that the ground, its drainage and its rivers reach the world and change over the steps. examples/eroding-island.yaml runs the erosion on a made-up island that comes with it ( island.npy ), a million years in 100 steps: cd ../go-simulator go run ./cmd/simulate -rules ../go-simulator-terrain/examples/eroding-island.yaml -output results/

how-it-works.title: 🔍 How it works

sections.text: How the plugin fits Go Simulator

how-it-works.text: 🔍 How it works How the plugin fits Go Simulator Go Simulator is the host. It keeps the world and moves the clock. The terrain plugin is a separate program the host starts; they talk over standard input and output (Go Simulator's protocol ). At the start the plugin describes itself: one rule, relief , its parameters, that it reads nothing from other plugins and that it writes elevation and slope . That description is also where the rules reference comes from. When the stage starts, the rule reads the relief, lays it on the world (see formats ), measures the slope of every cell (see how the slope is measured ) and sets both fields. Other plugins read the ground from the world, as the fields elevation and slope , instead of loading the file themselves. Put the terrain plugin first: plugins start in order, so the ones after it find the ground already there. A plugin never touches the renderer: it reads its copy of the world and answers with changes (Go Simulator's writing plugins ). Fields are in physical units and shapes in world units, as Go Simulator's vocabulary lists. What happens at every step On its own the ground does not change with time. The relief rule publishes it once, when the stage starts, so every plugin has it before its first step; if a host did not call the start, the first step publishes it instead. Every later step answers with nothing. The erosion rule , put after it, is the one that changes the ground over the steps. The picture is a real run: a stage from 0 to 3 with the island of the other pages, where simulate printed 0 changes for every step and the snapshots taken after steps 1 and 3 hold byte-identical fields. How the pictures were made The pictures of the island (the map at the top of the README, the two fields, and the profile along A–B) were drawn from the plugin's own answers. A small throwaway program, kept outside the repository, wrote a made-up island as a relieve.json and relieve.f32 , 160 × 110 cells of 50 m, from a few smooth hills and some noise, and the same heights as a .npy . Go Simulator's simulate ran the real plugin on both, and a second throwaway program drew the snapshot files it wrote: the elevation shaded and coloured by height with a line every 50 m, the slope on its own scale, and one row of both as a profile. The maps are PNG pairs, one for light and one for dark mode; the profile is an SVG with its own light and dark colours. They are 2D drawings, not screenshots of Go Simulator's viewer: the viewer draws the scene's own ground, not these fields. The diagrams (how it fits, the slope of a row, placing a relief, the steps) were drawn by hand in the same style; the numbers in the slope diagram were checked against the plugin's own code. The older island further down reliefs and fields comes from the earlier docs.

overview.title: Welcome to Go Terrain Simulator 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Terrain Simulator 👋 The terrain plugin gives a simulated world its ground , and lets rivers carve it over thousands of years: valleys, ridges, coasts. It reads a relief (a grid of heights) into the world, and its erosion rule lets the ground change: the earth pushes it up, rivers wear it down, slopes round off. Other plugins (climate, flora, towns) read the ground it leaves. Is it for me? ✅ You use Go Simulator and want ground shaped by water and time . ✅ You want to set it up by writing a rules file : no programming needed. ✅ You are curious about the science behind it: the pages explain the model with pictures. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want to see it work 🏴‍☠️ The quest : an island shaped by its rivers, in 5 levels 45 min want to run its example Getting started 10 min want to know how erosion works Erosion and rivers 15 min are looking up a parameter Rules reference — All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest Getting started Understand Reliefs and fields Erosion and rivers How it works Reference Rules reference 🚧 Not done yet The erosion rule only cuts and rounds: no sediment is laid down (no deltas, alluvial fans or filled valleys), uplift is the same everywhere, and every rock gives way alike (one erodibility for the whole map). Without it, the relief is read and published once. No aspect (which way a slope faces) and no catchments; the flow itself only shows as drainage_area and the rivers. .npy reliefs must be two-dimensional little-endian float32 or float64 arrays in C order; Fortran-ordered arrays are refused. The cells are square: a relief with different spacings east and north cannot be read. examples/ground.yaml does not come with a relief: put your own relieve.json and relieve.f32 next to it (see getting started ). Go Simulator's 3D viewer draws the scene's own ground, not these fields, so there are no screenshots of the viewer here; the pictures are 2D drawings of the published fields (see how the pictures were made ). Words you will meet Word What it means Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Plugin A small program that adds one ability to another: here, one kind of simulation each. Rules file A text file (YAML) that says which plugins to use, with which numbers, for how long: no programming needed. Field A grid of numbers laid over the world: the height of every spot, its temperature, its rain. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go Terrain Simulator is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator (this one) ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

reliefs-and-fields.title: 🏔️ Reliefs and fields
reliefs-and-fields.text: 🏔️ Reliefs and fields Almost every simulator needs to know the shape of the land: the climate to know where it is cold, the forests to know where it is too steep, the town to know where it can build. Instead of each one loading its own copy of the relief (and maybe disagreeing about it), the terrain plugin reads it once and puts it in the world for everyone. Put it first in the rules file: plugins start in order, so the ones after it find the ground already there. What it publishes At the start, two fields of the vocabulary : Field Unit How elevation metres the relief's heights, untouched slope rise over run the gradient like numpy.gradient : central differences inside, one-sided at the edges Values sit at cell centres, rows from the smallest z and columns from the smallest x. The relief rule publishes them once: on its own the ground does not change, so later steps publish nothing. To let it change, add the erosion rule after it: the land rises, the rivers cut their valleys and the hillslopes round off, and the rule publishes the ground again as it changes, with drainage_area and the rivers. Another made-up island, shaded, and its two fields: How the slope is measured Every cell gets two rises over run, one along the row (x) and one along the column (z), taken like numpy.gradient : half the difference between the two neighbours inside the grid, and the difference with the only neighbour at the edges. The slope is the length of those two, √(along_x² + along_z²) . The numbers in the picture are what the plugin's own code gives for that row. The distance between cells is in metres, so the slope is a true rise over run: the cell size in world units times metres_per_unit (1000 by default, for scenes in kilometres). A slope of 1 is a 45° flank. Formats The rule tells the two apart by the end of path : .json or .npy . Go Scene Builder's relief relieve.json , {"columns", "rows", "cell", "west", "north", "units"} , with the heights in metres as little-endian float32 in relieve.f32 next to it, row by row from the north. Its coordinates are kilometres east and north; origin places it on the world: x = east − origin[0] , z = origin[1] − north . Rows go from the north, which is the smallest z, so no row is flipped. - rule: relief with: {path: relieve.json, origin: [6, 4.5]} NumPy array A two-dimensional .npy of float32 or float64 heights in metres, rows from the smallest z, placed by the centre of its first cell and the spacing of its cells, in world units. - rule: relief with: {path: relief.npy, minimum_x: -1, minimum_z: -1, cell_size: 0.0125} metres_per_unit (1000 for scenes in kilometres) turns the cell size into metres for the slope. The island in these pictures was written both ways, as a relieve.json with origin: [4, 2.75] and as a .npy with minimum_x: -3.975 , minimum_z: -2.725 and cell_size: 0.05 ; the two runs published byte-identical fields. Exactness The field's extent is float64, so a plugin that rebuilds the grid from the field gets the same cell size and cell centres as the file. This matters for simulations that are sensitive to their inputs: a tenth of a millimetre of difference in the heights can grow a different town.

rules-reference.title: 📋 Rules of the terrain plugin
rules-reference.text: 📋 Rules of the terrain plugin Version 0.2.0, protocol 2. Publishes the ground of a relief as fields of the world, elevation (m) and slope (m/m), and can evolve it: uplift, rivers and hillslopes. This reference is generated from what the plugin itself tells the host (the describe message), so it always matches the code. Parameters go under with: in a rules file; see Go Simulator's rules file reference . Rule What it does relief Reads a relief and publishes, at the start, the fields elevation (metres) and slope (rise over run). erosion Evolves the ground the world already has: uplift, rivers that cut valleys (stream power) and hillslopes that round off (diffusion). Publishes elevation, slope, drainage_area (km²) and the rivers, at the start and as the ground changes. relief Reads a relief and publishes, at the start, the fields elevation (metres) and slope (rise over run). Reads: nothing from other plugins Writes: elevation , slope Parameter Type Default Meaning path text relief: relieve.json (with relieve.f32 next to it) or a .npy array of heights in metres origin list .json reliefs: [east, north] of the world's origin; x = east − origin[0], z = origin[1] − north minimum_x number .npy reliefs: x of the first column's cell centres (world units) minimum_z number .npy reliefs: z of the first row's cell centres (world units) cell_size number .npy reliefs: spacing of the cells (world units) metres_per_unit number 1000 size of a world unit in metres, for the slope erosion Evolves the ground the world already has: uplift, rivers that cut valleys (stream power) and hillslopes that round off (diffusion). Publishes elevation, slope, drainage_area (km²) and the rivers, at the start and as the ground changes. Reads: fields elevation Writes: elevation , slope , drainage_area , river Parameter Type Default Meaning years_per_unit number 1 years of erosion each unit of the stage's clock stands for (10000: every step is ten thousand years) uplift number 0 metres a year the land rises erodibility number 1e-05 K of the stream power law, a year⁻¹ · m^(1−2m) area_exponent number 0.5 m of the stream power law (the slope's exponent is 1) diffusivity number 0.005 m² a year: how fast hillslopes round off sea_level number 0 metres: lower ground is sea and does not change river_area number 1 km² drained from which there is a river river_width list [metres, exponent]: width = metres · area(km²)^exponent; default [3, 0.5] random_receivers boolean false water goes to a lower neighbour drawn by its slope, not always the steepest: no straight valleys along the grid seed number 1 seed of random_receivers: the same seed, the same valleys publish_every number 1 steps between publications of the changed ground metres_per_unit number 1000 size of a world unit in metres

the-quest.title: The terrain quest
the-quest.text: The terrain quest Shape an island with water and time, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of the terrain plugin and ends with a new island to look at in 3D. The quest map: a road from START through 5 levels — Surveyor, Rainmaker, Mountain builder, Meanderer and Coast keeper — to a final challenge, Island shaper We start from a smooth volcano of your own, 800 metres high, and let rivers find their way down it, uplift push it up, valleys wander, and the sea hold its coast, until two million years have made a mountain island. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the rules , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . Before you start You need Go 1.25 and GEOS ( sudo apt install libgeos-dev , brew install geos ), for looking at the results with Go Scene Builder. Clone the projects side by side, and make a folder for the quest: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-scene-builder git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-simulator-terrain mkdir island && cd island go mod init example.com/island Looking at a result The plugin publishes fields : a grid of numbers over the world, such as the height of every cell. A run without a window writes each field in Go Scene Builder's relief format, so the builder can turn it into a 3D scene for Go Renderer's viewer. Three files do it, made once: view.yaml , how the island looks (green low down, rock higher, snow at the top, a sea at 0 m, the rivers as water): units: m chunk: 2 environment: {sun: [220, 35], water_level: 0} terrain: {color: "#7f9a4e", bands: [{above: 250, color: "#8a8674", blend: 80}, {above: 600, color: "#e9e7e1", blend: 60}]} rules: - when: {kind: river} shape: {role: water, width: "width * 1000"} look/main.go , which tells the builder how a snapshot's map is written (kilometres, with z growing to the south): // Command look turns a snapshot's entities into a map go-scene-builder reads: the snapshot writes // [x, z] in kilometres, with z to the south, and the builder needs to be told so. // // go run ./look "results/island 100.geojson" map.geojson package main import ( "encoding/json" "log" "os" ) func main() { content, err := os.ReadFile(os.Args[1]) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } var collection map[string]any if err := json.Unmarshal(content, &collection); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } properties, _ := collection["properties"].(map[string]any) if properties == nil { properties = map[string]any{} } properties["units"], properties["axes"] = "km", "east-south" collection["properties"] = properties out, _ := json.Marshal(collection) if err := os.WriteFile(os.Args[2], out, 0o644); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } And the three commands, after every run (here for the snapshot at time 100 of the stage island ): go run ./look "results/island 100.geojson" map.geojson go run ../go-scene-builder/cmd/build-scene -map map.geojson -relief "results/island 100 elevation.json" -style view.yaml -out island.glb go run ../go-renderer/cmd/visor island.glb The pictures were taken with -zoom 0.75 in the viewer. Level 1 · The Surveyor Mission Pieces Time A volcano of your own, in the world the relief format, the relief rule, fields, snapshots 10 min The idea A relief is a chessboard of heights : every square says how high the ground is. It lives in two files, a small label ( relieve.json : how many squares, how big, where) and the heights themselves ( relieve.f32 : one number per square, row by row from the north). The relief rule reads it and puts it in the world as two fields : elevation (metres) and slope (how steep, rise over run). Other plugins read those fields; the terrain plugin's other rule will change them. Build it island/main.go writes the volcano, 8 × 8 km in cells of 50 m: // Command island writes a made-up island: relieve.json, the grid's size and place in kilometres, // and relieve.f32, a height in metres for every cell, row by row from the north. package main import ( "encoding/binary" "encoding/json" "log" "math" "os" ) func main() { const ( columns, rows = 160, 160 // cells cell = 0.05 // kilometres a side: 50 m west, north = -4.0, 4.0 ) heights := make([]float32, 0, columns*rows) for row := range rows { for column := range columns { east := west + (float64(column)+0.5)*cell northing := north - (float64(row)+0.5)*cell heights = append(heights, float32(height(east, northing))) } } header, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{"columns": columns, "rows": rows, "cell": cell, "west": west, "north": north, "units": "km"}) if err := os.WriteFile("relieve.json", header, 0o644); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } file, err := os.Create("relieve.f32") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } defer file.Close() if err := binary.Write(file, binary.LittleEndian, heights); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // height is a volcano-shaped island 800 m high, a little lopsided, under the sea at its edges. func height(east, north float64) float64 { distance := math.Hypot(east*1.2, north) // wider east to west shoulder := math.Max(0, 1-distance/3.2) // ridges and hollows of a few sizes, so the rivers have somewhere to start bumps := 60*math.Sin(east*2.3+1)*math.Cos(north*1.7) + 30*math.Sin(east*5.1)*math.Sin(north*4.3+2) + 15*math.Cos(east*9.7+north*8.9) return 820*math.Pow(shoulder, 1.6) + bumps*shoulder - 30 } go run ./island rules.yaml , one stage of one step that snapshots the world at its end: plugins: - name: terrain command: [go, run, .] directory: ../go-simulator-terrain stages: - name: ground clock: {from: 0, to: 1, step: 1} snapshots: [1] rules: - rule: relief with: {path: relieve.json, origin: [0, 0]} go run ../go-simulator/cmd/simulate -rules rules.yaml -output results/ Checkpoint results/ holds ground 1 elevation.json and .f32 , ground 1 slope.json and .f32 . Look at the elevation (the snapshot is ground 1 ): a smooth cone in the sea, green at the shore, rock on its shoulders, snow on top. Level 1: a smooth volcano in the sea Bonus (optional): two peaks Achievement unlocked: Surveyor Learn more: Reliefs and fields · Rules Level 2 · The Rainmaker Mission Pieces Time Rivers that find their way down and cut valleys the erosion rule, years per step, drainage 8 min The idea Pour a glass of water on a sandcastle: it runs down the steepest way, gathers in gullies, and the more water a gully carries, the faster it digs. That is the stream power law : erosion grows with the area a river drains and the slope it runs down. Over thousands of years, gullies become valleys. Each step of the clock stands for as many years as years_per_unit says: 100 steps of 10,000 years are a million. Build it A stage of 100 steps, with the relief first and erosion after it: plugins: - name: terrain command: [go, run, .] directory: ../go-simulator-terrain stages: - name: island clock: {unit: year, from: 0, to: 100, step: 1} snapshots: [0, 100] snapshot_fields: [elevation, drainage_area] rules: - rule: relief with: {path: relieve.json, origin: [0, 0]} - rule: erosion with: {years_per_unit: 10000, erodibility: 0.000002, river_area: 0.3} river_area says from how many km² drained a stream counts as a river: those become entities of kind river , which look puts on the map. Checkpoint The run takes a second or two. At 100, the volcano is lower and scored by gullies, with rivers down to the sea. Level 2: the volcano worn lower, rivers running to the sea Bonus (optional): softer rock Achievement unlocked: Rainmaker Learn more: How it works · Erosion Level 3 · The Mountain builder Mission Pieces Time Uplift that pushes the island up as the rivers wear it down uplift 5 min The idea An escalator going up while you walk down: if you walk as fast as it climbs, you stay where you are. Mountains are like that: the earth pushes them up, rivers wear them down, and they settle where the two balance. Build it The erosion rule's parameters only: with: {years_per_unit: 10000, uplift: 0.0002, erodibility: 0.000002, river_area: 0.3} 0.0002 m a year is 2 metres every 10,000 years. Checkpoint The island grows taller , the snow reaches lower, and the valleys run straight from the top, like the spokes of a wheel: water always takes the steepest of the eight neighbours of a cell, so it follows the grid. Level 3: a taller island with straight valleys like spokes Bonus (optional): find the balance Achievement unlocked: Mountain builder Level 4 · The Meanderer Mission Pieces Time Valleys that wander, the same every run random_receivers , seed 5 min The idea Real water does not always take the single steepest way: a pinball bounces down a slope, more often down the steeper side, never quite the same line. With random_receivers , water picks a lower neighbour by chance, weighted by its slope . The seed makes the chance repeatable: the same seed, the same valleys. Build it with: {years_per_unit: 10000, uplift: 0.0002, erodibility: 0.000002, river_area: 0.3, random_receivers: true, seed: 7} Checkpoint The spokes are gone: valleys bend and join as on a real mountain. Run it twice: the two islands are identical. Change the seed: other valleys. Level 4: valleys that bend and join Bonus (optional): rounder hills Achievement unlocked: Meanderer Level 5 · The Coast keeper Mission Pieces Time A sea level the rivers stop at sea_level 4 min The idea A river stops cutting where it meets the sea: the sea is its floor . Ground under sea_level is sea, and does not change, so the coast holds while the land above it is carved. Build it with: {years_per_unit: 10000, uplift: 0.0002, erodibility: 0.000002, river_area: 0.3, random_receivers: true, seed: 7, sea_level: 60} Checkpoint Below 60 m, a ring of the old smooth slope stays as it was, a green shore round the island; above it, the valleys reach down to it. Level 5: a smooth green shore round the carved island Achievement unlocked: Coast keeper Learn more: Rules: erosion Final challenge · Island shaper Run two million years on the volcano, with uplift, wandering valleys, rounder hills and a sea at 20 m, and snapshot the start, the middle and the end. Then look at the start and the end side by side. Hint: 200 steps of 10,000 years; three snapshots; all the parameters of levels 2 to 5, a lower river_area for more rivers. Try it on your own first, then compare with the solution. The start: the smooth volcano The end: two million years later, a mountain island with snow and valleys to every shore Rare achievement unlocked: Island shaper Well done All six achievements: Surveyor, Rainmaker, Mountain builder, Meanderer, Coast keeper and Island shaper You made a relief, put it in a world, and wore it into a mountain with the same laws real geomorphologists use.
